title: Ten Things to Understand About Research and Reading Instruction
author: Dr. Andy Johnson
summary: Andy Johnson, author of Making Sense of the Science of Reading: Context Matters, answers the demand for research by first laying out ten ideas about what educational research can and cannot do. He argues that research answers narrow questions in specific contexts, that single studies support points without proving them, and that a claim of superiority requires peer-reviewed comparisons of equivalent groups. On that last point he asserts that the Science of Reading movement has not yet produced such comparisons. His practical complaint is access: Minnesota teachers are told to apply research-informed practice yet are denied a legitimate research database, which he says leaves them dependent on what others tell them. He also dismisses ERIC and What Works Clearinghouse as inadequate databases, a claim he states rather than demonstrates. The piece closes by proposing database subscriptions as cheaper and more lasting professional development than the commercial training programs approved in Minnesota, whose effectiveness he says is unsupported. It is a polemic from a critic of the movement, useful for its framing of research literacy even where its assertions are contested.
points: Johnson frames research as a bounded snapshot of a specific time, place, and sample, so findings should not be generalized without checking context.
His standard for comparative claims is demanding: you can only say one approach beats another if peer-reviewed studies compared equivalent groups using each.
He treats teacher access to a real research database as a precondition for evidence-based practice, which turns a rhetorical argument into a concrete procurement question.

The closing proposal is that database subscriptions would be cheaper and longer-lasting professional development than branded training programs, though the claim about those programs having no supporting research is his own.
The reminder that reading research also needs instructional scaffolding is a useful prompt for how schools might train teachers to evaluate studies.
quotes: Research answers specific research questions and is used to validate specific research hypotheses. It is a snapshot taken of a small slice of reality, set in the context of a specific time and place, with specific conditions, participants, and methodology.
A single study can support a point, but it does not prove a point. When looking at research, you can’t look at a single study to determine anything conclusively.

For example, to conclude that structured literacy is more effective than balanced literacy instruction, you’d want the conclusion to be based on peer-reviewed research comparing two groups, one using structured literacy and the other using balanced literacy. And the groups must be equivalent in terms of demographics and conditions.

How are teacher supposed to know what research-based reading instruction is or to make research-based decisions if they are denied access to research? How are they supposed to know what a body of research says about something if they are not provided access to a body of research?
Unless and until every school has a subscription to a legitimate research database similar to those found at most universities, the Science of Reading advocate are merely making noise.

One of the most economical and efficient forms of professional development for teachers would include providing them with access to a legitimate database of research and scholarly articles. Subscriptions to these databases would cost far less and would have a far more lasting impact than the very expensive commercialized professional development programs that are being used here in Minnesota.

You can’t expect to read a research article in the same way you’d read a Harry Potter book. Much like initial reading instruction, learning how to read and evaluate research articles takes time, some instructional scaffolding, and practice.
